entry.englishMeaning: referring to a decision or commitment previously accepted

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Discourse phrase referring back to a previous agreement; here, the agreed timing of the first review.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral, but it can emphasize that a commitment already exists.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Confirming and matter-of-fact here: it restates the Monday review arrangement.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in workplace messages and ordinary planning. Use it only when an agreement was actually reached.

when_to_use: Confirm a delivery date that both parties accepted yesterday. A model in this sense: As agreed, we will each pay half the repair cost.
when_not_to_use: Do not write as agreed when the other person has not accepted the proposal. Use as proposed or ask for confirmation instead.

advanced_nuance: As agreed can confirm a shared plan or remind someone of a commitment. Its tone depends on the surrounding message; in a dispute, it may sound firm rather than friendly.
As agreed assumes prior acceptance. It should not be used to turn silence or an unaccepted suggestion into an agreement.

memory_practice.memory_sentence: As agreed, we will each pay half the repair cost.
memory_practice.production_task: Confirm a delivery date that both parties accepted yesterday. Respond in one or two natural sentences using the expression, then compare with the pattern after answering.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: referring to a decision or commitment previously accepted. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: You suggested Monday, but the other person has not replied. Can you accurately write As agreed, we will meet on Monday? Explain what evidence is missing.

examples.scenario: As agreed, the first review will take place on Monday.
examples.another_setting: As agreed, we will each pay half the repair cost.

A: As agreed, we will each pay half the repair cost.
B: Yes; send me the invoice and I will transfer my share.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: As agreed, the first review will take place on Monday.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: referring to a decision or commitment previously accepted
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker confirms Monday as the date already accepted for the first review. As agreed refers back to that shared decision rather than presenting a new proposal.

mistakes_differences.correction: As agreed, the price is fixed.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: As agree, the price is fixed.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Agreed implies acceptance; proposed only indicates a suggestion.

entry.englishMeaning: a continuous sequence or flow of events or things
entry.coreIdea: Things follow one another like a continuing flow.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative noun for a continuing sequence, comparing life's recurring difficulties with flowing water.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral as a sequence word; “never-ending” and “collisions” make this particular stream sound troublesome.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Reflective and dramatic here: the writer uses a continuous series of collisions to discuss personal responsibility.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in general writing and conversation. In this entry it does not name a physical watercourse.

when_to_use: Describe things or events arriving or happening one after another in a continuing flow.
when_not_to_use: Do not use a stream of to describe just one isolated event.
If the exact number or timing matters, give those details; stream alone does not measure them.

advanced_nuance: Stream suggests continuity but does not require a perfectly regular rate. A steady stream adds the idea of sustained or fairly consistent flow.
The noun after of establishes what is flowing. In the source, stream of head-on collisions is a dramatic image for repeated clashes, not a literal water description.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture messages arriving one after another along a flowing line.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: A steady stream of visitors arrived throughout the afternoon.
memory_practice.recall_question: What does a stream of visitors emphasize beyond a group of visitors?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Ten visitors arrive together once; other visitors keep arriving throughout the day. Which situation is better described as a steady stream? Explain the continuing-flow idea.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a short update to a fictional event organizer describing a stream of visitors or questions. Add one practical response to the continuing arrivals.

examples.example_1: A steady stream of visitors arrived throughout the afternoon.
examples.example_2: She could not finish the report because a stream of messages kept interrupting her.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Have the questions stopped coming in?
B: No, there is still a steady stream of messages.
A: Let’s collect the repeated questions into one reply.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Although  it' s  true  that  there  are  times  when  we  are  merely  bystanders  in  life's  never-ending  stream  of  head-on  collisions,  rarely are  we  completely  in nocent .
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: a continuous sequence or flow of events or things
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The writer pictures life’s recurring conflicts as a never-ending flow of collisions. Stream describes the continuing sequence; the dramatic image does not mean that literal water or road crashes are involved.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: A steady stream visitors entered the hall.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say A steady stream of visitors entered the hall. Use of to introduce what makes up the flow.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: A group describes items considered together. A stream emphasizes their continuing arrival or movement, one after another.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: a stream of + plural noun/uncountable noun; a steady/constant stream of + things

semanticReview.finding: Continuous-sequence noun sense taught with concrete arrival examples; source collision metaphor not literalized.
